title: The Alderman of Warsaw: the Bund, the Comintern, and a Grave With Nothing In It
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Mlawa, and the House That Moved to Warsaw

stops.name: Mlawa, the youngest of fourteen
stops.date_confidence: Year attested; day and month disputed and unresolved. English-language reference works give 1890 with no day. The Polish Wikipedia article gives 20 December 1890 and names the mother as Syma nee Horn. The 7 February date carried here comes from the dossier tradition and was not confirmed by any source that could be refetched. The Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon confirms the wealthy Hasidic family and the fourteen children; it does not call the father a timber merchant, which is a separate and uncorroborated detail.
stops.campa: In Mlawa, a market town of the Plock Governorate under Russian rule, a son is born to Yisroel Alter, of a wealthy Hasidic family, and to his wife Syma. He is the youngest of fourteen children. The house keeps the observance of its province and the boy will carry none of it forward: inside twenty years he is a Bundist and an engineer. The record of Mlawa keeps almost nothing else of him, not a street, not a schoolroom, and the birth date itself is disputed, February in one tradition and December in another. What he took out of that house was the language.
suggested_refs: The Jewish quarter of Mlawa in the Plock Governorate, Russian Poland, 1890
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

stops.name: Warsaw, the stepfather who was a maskil
stops.date_confidence: The move to Warsaw and the mother's remarriage to Israel Wolf Gliksman, described by the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon as a maskil and an early Zionist, are attested; the lexicon dates neither. The claim that the father died when Wiktor was about one year old, and the 1891 date used here, are dossier tradition and could not be corroborated on refetch. The year orders the segment and should not be quoted as a fact.
stops.campa: The father dies and the widow takes her children to Warsaw. She marries again, and the second husband is no Hasid. Israel Wolf Gliksman is a maskil and an early sympathizer of Zionism, so the Enlightenment enters the house by way of a stepfather. The boy grows up inside an argument about what the Jews of Poland are to become, a faith or a nation, and he will answer it with a third word, the one the Bundists use for the country a people already lives in. Doikayt. Hereness. The lexicon that records the remarriage gives it no date.
suggested_refs: The Warsaw maskilic milieu of the 1890s, into which the Alter children were transplanted from Hasidic Mlawa
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

stops.name: Wojciech Gorski Gymnasium, the strike at fifteen
stops.date_confidence: The 1905 school strike, the brief arrest, and joining the Bund in 1905 are attested by Polish Wikipedia and by the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon. The consequence is contradicted between sources and is left open: the lexicon says he lost his place at the school, while the Polish Wikipedia article on the gymnasium itself lists Alter among its graduates. Month and day of the strike are not established; January orders the segment. Coordinates corrected to ul. Wojciecha Gorskiego, formerly ul. Hortensji, per Nominatim; the dossier value sat some 780 m south.
stops.campa: The private gymnasium on Hortensji Street teaches in Polish, secular and expensive, and in the revolutionary year its pupils strike. Alter is fifteen and in the street with them; the police take him, hold him a short while, and let him go. That same year he joins the Bund, the Jewish workers' party that organizes in Yiddish and is hunted in Yiddish. One account says the school stripped him of the right to continue there. Another lists him among its own graduates. Whether he ever finished at Hortensji Street is not known.
suggested_refs: Gimnazjum Wojciecha Gorskiego, ul. Hortensji 2, Warsaw, and the school strikes of the 1905 Revolution
sources: Polish Wikipedia, 'Gimnazjum Wojciecha Gorskiego w Warszawie'
Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

stops.name: Liege, the polytechnic
stops.date_confidence: Belgian engineering study is attested across four sources. The 1906 start date appears in none of them and is inferred from the lexicon's own sequence, arrest at fifteen in 1905 and a degree in 1910; treat it as approximate. The Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon is the only source naming a Liege polytechnic and an electromechanical degree completed in 1910, and it is contradicted by the Ghent tradition recorded at the next stop.
stops.campa: He crosses Europe to study engineering in a country with no Pale of Settlement and no quota on Jews at the polytechnic. Liege is furnaces, coal, and drawing boards; he learns machines properly, and the trade will feed him later in a London factory and mark him for good as a Bundist who could read a balance sheet and a boiler with the same eye. The lexicon of his own movement says he finished in 1910 as an electromechanical engineer. Around him in the Belgian cities are other students out of Russian Poland, carrying on the same arguments in exile.
suggested_refs: The Liege polytechnic and the Russian-Jewish student emigration to Belgium before 1914
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

stops.name: Ghent, the disputed diploma
stops.date_confidence: A genuine and unresolved conflict, presented as such. English and Russian Wikipedia give mechanical engineering at the University of Ghent, 1912; the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon gives an electromechanical degree from a Liege polytechnic, 1910; Polish Wikipedia gives both cities. No source reached adjudicates between them. The 1912 date here belongs to the Ghent version only.
stops.campa: A second tradition puts the diploma here instead: mechanical engineering, the University of Ghent, 1912. The Polish accounts split the difference and give him both cities. Nothing reachable adjudicates it, and the two versions differ by two years and by a discipline. What is not in dispute is the shape of the thing. He comes out of Belgium with an engineer's title, which in Congress Poland puts him in a class the Bund rarely recruited from. Then he goes back to Warsaw, where the party is illegal.
suggested_refs: The Ghent and Liege engineering registers for 1910-1912, unexamined here and the obvious place to settle the dispute

stops.name: Brussels, Melanie Lorraine
stops.date_confidence: The marriage to a Belgian woman named Melanie Lorraine is attested by the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon, which gives no date. The 1911-1912 dating, the Brussels residence, and her death there in 1974 come from a family correction recorded in the dossier and were not independently verified; Brussels is a plausible but unconfirmed placement.
stops.campa: In Belgium he marries Melanie Lorraine, a Belgian woman, and the marriage runs in two directions at once. He returns to Warsaw, to the underground, to a Tsarist prison, to Siberia. She stays where she is. A correction lodged by the family, confirmed by nothing else consulted, says she lives out her life in Brussels and dies there in 1974, thirty-one years after a Soviet executioner shot her husband in a town on the Volga she had likely never heard anyone name.
suggested_refs: Belgian civil registers for the Alter-Lorraine marriage, not consulted here
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

segments.name: The Underground, Siberia, and the London Exile

stops.name: Warsaw, the return and the April arrest
stops.date_confidence: The April 1913 arrest for Bund activity is attested by Polish Wikipedia, English Wikipedia, and the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon; the day within April is not given anywhere reached and defaults to the first. The return to Warsaw and the post with a Jewish cultural organization are attested by the lexicon. The 1913 joint workers'-insurance electoral committee with the SDKPiL and the PPS-Lewica is dossier-cited lexicon material that could not be refetched.
stops.campa: Back in Warsaw with his diploma, he takes a post with a Jewish cultural organization and keeps the illegal work running underneath it: committees, strike funds, the party press. In 1913 he sits for the Bund on a joint electoral committee for workers' insurance beside the SDKPiL and the PPS-Lewica, three rival Marxist parties agreeing on a sickness fund if on nothing else. In April the police take him. There is no trial worth the name, only an administrative order, and the order says Siberia.
suggested_refs: Tsarist administrative exile procedure for political suspects in Vistula Land, 1913
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

stops.name: Narym, exile and escape
stops.date_confidence: Exile to Siberia and a later escape to western Europe are attested. The specific placement at Narym is not: the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon says only that he was imprisoned and exiled to Siberia, and none of English, Polish, or Russian Wikipedia names a location. Narym comes from the dossier tradition alone and may not belong on the map at all. Coordinates corrected to the Nominatim value for Narym, Tomsk Oblast; the dossier value lay some 44 km north in empty taiga. The month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: Exile is not a sentence to a prison but a sentence to a distance: a village on a river in the Tomsk taiga, a stipend too small to live on, and a policeman who counts heads. Alter does not stay. He escapes, crosses the empire westward, and is out of Russia before the year ends. The lexicon of his own movement records only that he was imprisoned and exiled to Siberia. The particular village named here comes from tradition, and no source that could be reached repeats it.
suggested_refs: Narym, Tomsk Governorate, standing place of political exile; the placement here is unverified
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

stops.name: The Jewish East End, London, the laborer and the engineer
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon and by English and Polish Wikipedia: arrival in Britain after the outbreak of war, work first as a laborer then as an engineer, organizing among Yiddish-speaking workers through the group Veker. The month is a placeholder; no source reached dates the arrival more closely than 1914.
stops.campa: He reaches England in the first months of the war and starts at the bottom: a laborer's job, then work as an engineer in a factory, in the Yiddish-speaking streets of Whitechapel and Stepney where the immigrant trades run on piecework and the pubs argue politics until closing. The war has scattered the Russian revolutionary emigration across half of Europe and London holds its share. Alter organizes among the workers rather than among the exiles, through the socialist group Veker, which means the waker, the one who rouses people out of sleep.
suggested_refs: The Yiddish immigrant labor milieu of Whitechapel and Stepney, 1914-1917
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

stops.name: London, Arbeter-Vort and the campaign against conscription
stops.date_confidence: Writing for Arbeter-Vort, the campaign against conscription, and contact with anti-militarist socialists in the Labour Party circle are attested by English and Polish Wikipedia and by the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon. The 1916 date is an ordering device chosen because British conscription began that January; no source reached dates Alter's campaigning within the London years.
stops.campa: He writes for Arbeter-Vort, the workers' word, and campaigns against conscription in a country that has just begun to conscript. The question is exact and dangerous: Russian Jewish subjects living in Britain, men who fled the Tsar's army and the Tsar's police, are being pressed to fight for the Tsar's ally. Alter argues no. His allies are on the anti-militarist wing of the Labour Party, the first legal socialist movement he has ever worked inside. Conscription comes in that January regardless.
suggested_refs: Arbeter-Vort, London Yiddish socialist weekly, and the 1916 conscription controversy among Russian Jewish subjects in Britain
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

segments.name: Revolution, and the First Soviet Arrest

stops.name: Petrograd, back into the empire
stops.date_confidence: The return after the February Revolution and a short stay in Petrograd are attested by the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon; the dossier's fuller account of the itinerary is tradition that could not be refetched. The May date is an ordering device only, chosen to sit between February and the August conference at Kyiv.
stops.campa: The Tsar falls in February and the exiles come home from everywhere at once, by boat, by train, through Sweden and Finland. Alter returns from London into a capital where the Bund is suddenly legal: printing openly, standing in elections, quarreling with itself over the war and over the Bolsheviks. Soviets sit in the factories, a hundred parties put out newspapers, and nobody yet knows which of them will be permitted to exist in a year. He does not stay long. The party's work has scattered south and west with the empire's Jews, and he goes after it.
suggested_refs: The legalization of the Bund in Russia after February 1917
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

stops.name: Kyiv, the Southern Conference
stops.date_confidence: The Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon lists Kyiv among his 1917 stops. The August date and the description of him speaking for the Bund's Internationalist current come from the dossier tradition and were not independently refetched; day of month is a default.
stops.campa: At the Bund's Southern Conference in Kyiv he speaks for the Internationalists, the current that opposes the war outright and refuses the defencist position. The delegates come in from towns where the Bund holds the trade unions and the Zionists hold the schools. Ukraine in this summer is the densest Jewish country on earth and the most exposed; within two years its towns will be sites of pogroms that kill tens of thousands. None of that is in the room yet. The room is arguing about the war, and about a word in a resolution, and Alter is twenty-six.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the Bund's Southern Conference, Kyiv, August 1917
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

stops.name: Petrograd, elected to the Central Committee
stops.date_confidence: The December 1917 election to the Bund Central Committee at Petrograd is attested by Polish Wikipedia, English Wikipedia, and the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon. The designation 'Eighth Congress', carried by the dossier, is used by none of them and is not repeated here; the December 1917 Petrograd gathering is normally counted as the Bund's Eighth Conference. Day of month unrecorded.
stops.campa: In December the party gathers again in Petrograd, six weeks after the Bolshevik seizure of power, and elects Alter to its Central Committee. He is twenty-seven. The doctrine he inherits is Vladimir Medem's: national cultural autonomy, carried as Bund policy since the Warsaw resolution of 1912, a nation without a territory, secular, Yiddish, and at home where it already lives. Alter will spend twenty years administering that idea in a real city with real budgets. No source reached records the two men ever meeting.
suggested_refs: The Bund's Eighth Conference, Petrograd, December 1917, and the national-cultural-autonomy program adopted at Warsaw in August 1912
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

stops.name: Minsk, the Central Committee office and Der Veker
stops.date_confidence: Work at the Bund Central Committee's Minsk office, writing for the party daily Der Veker, and departure as German forces approached in 1918 are attested by the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon. Month and day are placeholders; the lexicon gives the period, not a date.
stops.campa: He works out of the Bund Central Committee's office in Minsk and writes for the party daily Der Veker. The territory changes hands around him: German armies, Bolshevik commissars, Polish troops, all inside three years, and the Jewish towns of Byelorussia are counted and requisitioned by each in turn. Minsk is one of the last places where the Bund works as a mass party inside Russia, answerable to no single ruling party. When the Germans close on the city he moves on again, in 1918, a year the lexicon gives without a month.
suggested_refs: Der Veker, Bund daily of Minsk, 1917-1918
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

stops.name: Moscow, the Cheka and the essay on Marx
stops.date_confidence: Two events merged into one stop at the same pin. The Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon places Alter in Moscow in this period; the Cheka arrest at a non-Bolshevik workers' conference, the threat of execution, and the release through Bolshevik intervention are dossier-cited Bundist accounts that could not be refetched. The essay 'Marks un di visnshaft fun geshikhte' in the anthology 'Zum ondenk fun Karl Marks' is a dossier bibliography citation, likewise unrefetched. July is the dossier's month for the arrest; the essay is dated only to 1918.
stops.campa: In Moscow he takes part in a conference of non-Bolshevik workers, the last sort of gathering the new state will tolerate, and the Cheka arrests the delegates. Bundist accounts say he faced execution and was let out through the intervention of prominent Bolsheviks. He stays on in the city afterward, translating from English and French into Russian and writing an essay for a Marx memorial volume, on Marx and the science of history. He writes it in the capital of the first state founded in Marx's name, under the eye of the police that had just held him.
suggested_refs: 'Marks un di visnshaft fun geshikhte', in 'Zum ondenk fun Karl Marks' (Moscow, 1918)
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'
Dossier-cited Bundist accounts of the July 1918 Cheka arrests, not independently refetched

segments.name: Warsaw Regained, and the Journey to Lenin's International

stops.name: Warsaw, return to independent Poland
stops.date_confidence: Attested, with a discrepancy of one year between sources on the starting point: English Wikipedia says he resided permanently in independent Poland from 1918 onward, while the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon frames the Warsaw leadership period as 1919-1939. The 1919 date is defensible and is used here for the segment; it should not be attributed to English Wikipedia, which gives 1918. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Poland exists again, and Alter comes back to it. He joins the Central Committee of the Polish Bund beside Henryk Erlich, and the two names will be printed together for the next twenty-four years and cut into one stone after that. The party they lead is not a sect. It runs unions, schools teaching in Yiddish, sports clubs, sanatoria, a children's organization, and daily papers, in a city where a third of the population is Jewish. English sources date his permanent residence in the new state to 1918; the Bundist lexicon starts the Warsaw period at 1919.
suggested_refs: The institutional network of the Polish Bund, 1919-1939: unions, TSYSHO schools, Medem sanatorium, SKIF
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

stops.name: Plac Bankowy, the councillor
stops.date_confidence: Better attested than the dossier's own tagging suggested. The Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon gives 'Warsaw City Council member (1919-1934)' verbatim, and Polish Wikipedia gives the aldermanic service as 1927-1936. Month and day of the first election are not recorded in anything reached. Coordinates corrected to the Nominatim value for Plac Bankowy; the dossier value lay some 280 m east, nearer Plac Teatralny.
stops.campa: Elected to the Warsaw City Council for the Bund, Alter walks into the municipal building on Plac Bankowy as a representative of a working-class Jewish electorate of several hundred thousand. What he does there is unglamorous and exact: housing, drainage, school subsidies, municipal jobs, hours and wages. His own movement's lexicon gives his council service as 1919 to 1934; the Polish record gives the aldermanic years as 1927 to 1936, and the two spans overlap without matching. He is twenty-nine at the first election.
suggested_refs: Warsaw municipal records of the Bund council delegation, 1919-1936
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

stops.name: Moscow, the Third Congress of the International
stops.date_confidence: The Third Congress of the Communist International sat in Moscow from 22 June to 12 July 1921, and its delegate table records the Bund in Poland sending three representatives, which corroborates the dossier's 'three Warsaw delegates'. The pseudonym 'M. Lorman' and the characterization of the mission as negotiating the Bund's affiliation are dossier-cited party history that could not be refetched, and the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon says nothing of either. The dossier had merged this congress with the 5 August arrest, three weeks its junior; the two are separated here.
stops.campa: He travels to Moscow in secret under the name M. Lorman, one of three delegates the Bund in Poland sends to the Third Congress of the Communist International. The pseudonym and the mission come from party history; the congress's own delegate table records only the number three. The question on the table is whether the Bund dissolves itself into Lenin's International on Lenin's conditions, which require it to surrender its press, its discipline, and its name. The congress sits from June into July. Alter carries home the refusal.
suggested_refs: Delegate roster and proceedings of the Third Congress of the Communist International, Moscow, 22 June to 12 July 1921
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Third Congress of the Communist International'
Dossier-cited Bundist party history for the pseudonym and the affiliation mission, not independently refetched

stops.name: Moscow, the nine-day hunger strike
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon: arrest on 5 August 1921 over Socialist-Revolutionary correspondence, a nine-day hunger strike, release. The detail that the letter described Bolshevik terror and was intended for Sylvia Pankhurst comes from the dossier's party-history material and could not be refetched.
stops.campa: On the fifth of August the Soviet authorities arrest him over a letter he is carrying, written by a Left Socialist-Revolutionary, describing Bolshevik terror, addressed by party tradition to Sylvia Pankhurst in London. He goes on hunger strike for nine days. They let him out. It is the second time Soviet police have held him and released him, and both times the reason is the same: he is a known name in the international socialist press, and in 1921 that still counts for something in Moscow.
suggested_refs: The Left Socialist-Revolutionary letter to Sylvia Pankhurst, cited in Bundist accounts of the August 1921 arrest
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

stops.name: Warsaw, the council of Jewish unions
stops.date_confidence: Dossier-cited institutional record, not independently refetched: service on the central trade-union commission and the chairmanship of the national council of Jewish unions in Poland from 1923. The Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon confirms his Warsaw leadership across this period but was not seen to give the union offices or the year. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Alter takes over the economic side of the party: the central trade-union commission from 1923, then the chairmanship of the national council of Jewish unions in Poland, both dated by institutional records that could not be refetched. Tailors, bakers, leather workers, printers, transport men, the trades that fill the Nalewki district and every small town with a market. This is the machinery that will make the Bund the leading Jewish party in Poland's municipal elections by the late 1930s, ahead of every Zionist list.
suggested_refs: Records of the national council of Jewish trade unions in Poland, 1923-1939
sources: Dossier-cited institutional record of the Bund's trade-union apparatus, not independently refetched

stops.name: Jerusalem, the report on Palestine
stops.date_confidence: The journey to Mandatory Palestine and the report published the following year as 'Der emes vegn Palestine' are dossier bibliography, and the Polish National Library catalogue does hold a 1925 edition of that title. The itinerary inside the country is entirely unestablished: Jerusalem is a plausible placement and no more, and no source reached names a city he visited. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: He travels through Mandatory Palestine to see the Zionist project standing up, and writes the report the following year: 'Der emes vegn Palestine', the truth about Palestine. His verdict is negative and it is not a religious verdict. The country is small, the Arab population is already there, and the Jewish masses of Poland number in the millions and will not be moved in time. Doikayt is the Bundist answer, and within two decades the argument will be settled by events rather than by debate. The route he took inside the country is not recorded.
suggested_refs: Wiktor Alter, 'Der emes vegn Palestine' (1925), held by the Polish National Library

stops.name: Plac Bankowy, the lawnik
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Polish Wikipedia, which gives the service as lawnik, a member of the city executive, from 1927 to 1936. Month and day of the appointment are not given. The coordinate is the corrected Nominatim value for Plac Bankowy.
stops.campa: From 1927 he sits as a lawnik, a member of the city executive, and the Polish record carries that service to 1936. Warsaw in these years holds more Jews than any city in Europe and more than any city on earth except New York. He signs the papers in Polish and argues over them in Yiddish. What the papers concern is relief funds, tenement inspections, municipal wages, and the sanitary state of courtyards on the Jewish streets where a workshop, a family, and a privy share one air shaft.
suggested_refs: The Warsaw magistracy rolls, 1927-1936, naming Alter among the lawnicy

stops.name: New York, the American mission
stops.date_confidence: The 1929 journey to the United States is attested: the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon records 'Traveled to United States (1929)'. The city is not. Nothing reached places him in New York specifically; the pin is set at the seat of the Bund's American representation as the least speculative placement. The dossier's only located trace is a digitized 1929 press notice advertising him at a San Francisco address, which could not be refetched, so the itinerary is a gap. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: He crosses the Atlantic on a Bund mission to the American Jewish labor movement: the world of the Forverts, the Workmen's Circle, and the garment unions, which sends money back to Poland and expects to be told plainly what it is buying. The Yiddish press advertises him as a Warsaw alderman and a leader of the Bund. One surviving notice from the tour comes from San Francisco, so his route ran well past the eastern cities. The notice itself could not be recovered and the itinerary remains a hole in the record.
suggested_refs: The 1929 Yiddish press notices of Alter's American tour, including the San Francisco advertisement digitized by the National Library of Israel
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'
Dossier summary of a National Library of Israel digitized 1929 press notice, not refetched

stops.name: Paris, how to bring about socialism
stops.date_confidence: 'Comment realiser le socialisme?' (Paris, 1932) is dossier bibliography and was not independently verified. The companion title 'Esquisse d'un programme economique socialiste' (Paris, 1934) is in neither the Polish National Library catalogue nor OpenLibrary and could not be verified at all; it is mentioned here without a date of its own. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: He publishes in French, in Paris, a book asking how socialism is actually to be brought about, and follows it with a sketch of a socialist economic program that turns up in no catalogue reached and may not exist at all. The question is not agitation but arithmetic: how a socialist government runs an economy on the morning after it takes office, what it takes into public hands first, what it does about the banks. The year is 1932. Polish unemployment is catastrophic, and across the border the German republic is in its last winter.
suggested_refs: Wiktor Alter, 'Comment realiser le socialisme?' (Paris, 1932); the companion 'Esquisse d'un programme economique socialiste' remains unverified in any catalogue reached
sources: Polish National Library catalogue, data.bn.org.pl (negative for the Esquisse)

stops.name: Warsaw, when the socialists come to power
stops.date_confidence: Attested by catalogue: the Polish National Library holds Alter, Wiktor, 'Gdy socjalisci dojda do wladzy...!', publisher Nowe Pismo, Warszawa, 1934. The same catalogue holds a 1935 pamphlet, 'Jednosc i plan', which the dossier bibliography omits. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: The Polish National Library holds the volume: Wiktor Alter, 'Gdy socjalisci dojda do wladzy...!', when the socialists come to power, Warsaw, the Nowe Pismo press, 1934. It is the Paris question restated in Polish for a Polish readership, in a state governed since 1926 by Pilsudski's sanacja and with no intention whatever of letting socialists come to power. The same catalogue holds a pamphlet from the year after that his standard bibliographies leave out.
suggested_refs: Polish National Library records for 'Gdy socjalisci dojda do wladzy...!' (Nowe Pismo, 1934) and 'Jednosc i plan' (Nowe Pismo, 1935)

stops.name: Warsaw, the unity resolution and Mysl Socjalistyczna
stops.date_confidence: Dossier-cited party history and institutional listing, not independently refetched: the resolution calling for organic unity of the socialist and Communist Internationals, the failed talks with the Communist Party of Poland, and the founding and editing of Mysl Socjalistyczna from 1935 to 1938. Month and day are placeholders and the two strands are merged into one stop.
stops.campa: Alter drafts a resolution calling for organic unity between the socialist and the Communist Internationals, one workers' movement in place of two, and opens talks with the Communist Party of Poland. The talks fail. He founds a journal, Mysl Socjalistyczna, socialist thought, and edits it for three years. Soviet police have arrested him twice by now and he is still arguing for unity with the movement that arrested him. Why the second arrest did not settle the question for him is not set down anywhere that was found.
suggested_refs: Runs of Mysl Socjalistyczna, Warsaw, 1935-1938
sources: Dossier-cited party history and institutional listing, not independently refetched

stops.name: Grzybowska Street, head of the kehilla
stops.date_confidence: Stronger than the dossier's own tagging: the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon says he was 'elected head of Warsaw Jewish community administration from 1936', not merely elected to its board, which is how the dossier's geography lens put it. Month and day unrecorded. Coordinates corrected to the prewar kehilla offices at Grzybowska 26/28 per Nominatim; the dossier value lay some 900 m east near Plac Grzybowski.
stops.campa: After a Bund advance at the polls he is elected head of the administration of the Warsaw Jewish religious community, the kehilla on Grzybowska Street: the body that levies the communal tax and pays for the ritual slaughterers, the cemeteries, and the religious schools. A secularist now presides over the budget of Jewish Warsaw, his own movement's lexicon dating the election to 1936 without a month, and turns that budget toward secular education, welfare, and labor. The Hasidic world his father was born into sits on the other side of the ledger. He is forty-six.
suggested_refs: The Warsaw kehilla offices at Grzybowska 26/28 and the 1936 communal elections
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

segments.name: The Last Warsaw Years and the Roads East

stops.name: Madrid, Spain in flames
stops.date_confidence: The journey to Republican Spain and the co-authored volume 'Hiszpania w ogniu: rok wojny domowej' with Julius Deutsch are dossier bibliography, and the Polish National Library catalogue holds the 1937 book. The itinerary inside Spain is not established by anything reached; Madrid is an unconfirmed placement. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: He goes to Republican Spain in the second year of the war, on a mission of socialist solidarity and as a journalist, and publishes with the Austrian socialist Julius Deutsch a Polish account of what he saw: 'Hiszpania w ogniu', Spain in flames, a year of civil war. What he finds is the argument of his own last fifteen years of print happening in a country under bombardment: socialists, Communists, anarchists, and a republic, fighting one war against fascism and several against each other. Where he traveled inside Spain is not established.
suggested_refs: Wiktor Alter and Julius Deutsch, 'Hiszpania w ogniu: rok wojny domowej' (Warsaw, 1937), held by the Polish National Library

stops.name: Warsaw, economic antisemitism in the light of figures
stops.date_confidence: Dossier bibliography citation for 'Antysemityzm gospodarczy w swietle cyfr' (Warsaw, 1937), not independently refetched, though the title appears in the summary bibliography carried by English Wikipedia. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: He answers the accusation with a table of figures. 'Antysemityzm gospodarczy w swietle cyfr', economic antisemitism in the light of numbers, takes the claim that the Jews of Poland are an unproductive element living off the nation and sets it against the occupational data. The boycott campaigns are running, the universities have ghetto benches, and ministers of the state speak of emigration as policy. Alter replies with an occupational census. The pamphlet appears in Warsaw in 1937.
suggested_refs: Wiktor Alter, 'Antysemityzm gospodarczy w swietle cyfr' (Warsaw, 1937)

stops.name: Warsaw, man in society
stops.date_confidence: Dossier bibliography citation for 'Der mentsh iz der gezelshaft' and 'Czlowiek w spoleczenstwie' (1938); the Polish National Library catalogue independently holds 'Czlowiek w spoleczenstwie', 1938. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: His last book before the war comes out in Yiddish and in Polish: man in society, on the individual and the social order. He is forty-eight. The party he directs runs the largest Jewish trade unions in Europe, takes the Jewish municipal seats of Warsaw outright, and fields a youth movement of tens of thousands. Eleven months after the book is printed the German army crosses the Polish border, and everything the Bund built in Poland has a year left to run.
suggested_refs: Wiktor Alter, 'Czlowiek w spoleczenstwie' / 'Der mentsh iz der gezelshaft' (1938)

stops.name: Warsaw, the ninth of September
stops.date_confidence: Dossier-cited wartime chronology, not independently refetched: the departure of the Bund leadership from Warsaw, the Central Committee's reversal ordering leaders back, and Alter learning of it on 9 September. The Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon confirms the eastward flight and the Lublin stop that follows, but was not seen to give this date.
stops.campa: The leadership leaves the city ahead of the German advance, and then reverses itself: on the ninth of September Alter learns that the Central Committee has ruled the leaders are to turn back and stand with the population. He is forty-nine, an alderman of a city under bombardment, with no council left to sit in. He starts back. The roads are impassable in both directions, jammed with refugees, strafed from the air, cut by an army moving faster than the government it is chasing. He never sees Warsaw again.
suggested_refs: Bundist accounts of the Central Committee's September 1939 evacuation order and its reversal
sources: Dossier-cited wartime chronology, not independently refetched
Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

stops.name: Lublin, one issue of the Lubliner Shtime
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon: blocked from returning to Warsaw, Alter reached Lublin and issued a single wartime number of the Yiddish paper Lubliner Shtime under bombardment. The dossier gives the issue's date as 14 September, which is the date used here.
stops.campa: In Lublin, under bombardment, Alter puts out a single issue of a Yiddish newspaper, the Lubliner Shtime, the voice of Lublin, dated the fourteenth of September 1939. There is no party press left, no telephone line worth using, no reliable news, and a Jewish population with nowhere to go. One sheet of Yiddish type, set in a city with a week of ordinary life still in front of it, is what the director of the Bund's economic apparatus can still produce. Then he goes east with everybody else.
suggested_refs: Lubliner Shtime, single wartime issue, 14 September 1939
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'
Dossier-cited wartime chronology for the issue date

stops.name: Kowel, the Red Army and the NKVD
stops.date_confidence: Arrival at Kowel on 17 September and the NKVD arrest there are attested by the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon and by English and Polish Wikipedia. The arrest date is contradicted between sources and is left open: Polish Wikipedia gives 26 September, English Wikipedia 29 September. The stop is dated to the arrival.
stops.campa: He reaches Kowel in Volhynia on the seventeenth of September, the day the Red Army crosses Poland's eastern border. There is now no direction left to run in. Within nine or twelve days, and the sources do not agree which, the NKVD arrests him in the town: not as a refugee but as Wiktor Alter, leader of the Bund, a Jewish socialist party that had refused to dissolve into the Communist International in 1921 and had spent eighteen years saying so in print. The file opened on him is a political file from the first page.
suggested_refs: NKVD arrest records for Kowel, September 1939
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

stops.name: Luck, the transfer
stops.date_confidence: Dossier tradition alone: the movement from Kowel through the Luck prison before onward transport to Moscow is confirmed by no source that could be reached. Month and day are placeholders. This is the least documented leg of Alter's life and is carried here rather than dropped, flagged as unsupported.
stops.campa: From Kowel he is moved through the prison system, first west and then east: Luck, then a transport to Moscow. This leg is the thinnest in the whole of his record and rests on tradition alone. The people arrested with him in the Soviet zone in these weeks run into the tens of thousands, Polish officers, officials, party men of every persuasion, and most of the paperwork on them will stay sealed for fifty years. No source reached puts Alter inside the Luck prison at all.
suggested_refs: Luck (Lutsk) prison, autumn 1939, in the NKVD transport chain from the annexed territories
sources: Dossier tradition, not confirmed by any source reached

stops.name: Butyrka, twenty months of interrogation
stops.date_confidence: The Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon gives 'Moscow prisons (September 1939 to September 1941)'; Polish Wikipedia names Butyrki specifically from 9 December 1939, which is the date used here. The dossier pinned this stop at the Lubyanka, some 3.4 km southeast, and that pin is not used. The claim that he wrote an essay on modern physics, 'Di naye fizik', in prison is not confirmed by anything reached and is carried only as tradition.
stops.campa: Twenty months in the Moscow prisons, from September 1939 to September 1941, and from the ninth of December in Butyrka. The interrogations go over the Bund's organization, its money, its foreign contacts, and its refusal of the Comintern; he is asked to sign and does not sign. The men holding him are the successor service to the Cheka that arrested him in 1918 and to the police that arrested him in 1921. Twice before, they let him go. What he expected of the third time is nowhere recorded.
suggested_refs: Butyrka prison, Moscow; NKVD investigation file on Wiktor Alter, 1939-1941
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

stops.name: Moscow, sentence of death and commutation
stops.date_confidence: The 20 July 1941 death sentence is attested by Polish Wikipedia, which names the Military Collegium of the USSR Supreme Court, and by the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon. The venue is not: no source reached states where the sentence was handed down, and the parallel cuts the other way, since Henryk Erlich's death sentence was pronounced at Saratov. The pin is Alter's known place of confinement, not an attested courtroom. The commutation is dated 22 July by Polish Wikipedia and 30 July elsewhere; both are recorded, neither is resolved.
stops.campa: On the twentieth of July 1941, four weeks after Germany invades the Soviet Union, the Military Collegium of the Supreme Court sentences Wiktor Alter to death for working on behalf of international fascist reaction: a Jewish socialist condemned as an agent of Hitler in the summer of the Einsatzgruppen. Two days later, or ten depending on which record is followed, the sentence is commuted to ten years in a labor camp. The state that condemned him has just acquired an urgent need for Polish allies.
suggested_refs: Military Collegium of the USSR Supreme Court, sentence of 20 July 1941, and the commutation of 22 or 30 July
sources: Congress for Jewish Culture, Yiddish biographical lexicon, 'Alter, Viktor'

stops.name: Moscow, released under the amnesty
stops.date_confidence: Release under the amnesty following the Sikorski-Mayski agreement is attested by English and Polish Wikipedia, the latter giving 13 September. The apology, the hotel, the clothing and medical care, and the offer of an international Jewish anti-Hitler committee with Erlich as chairman and Alter as secretary come from Albert Glotzer's March 1943 account, which is contemporaneous and partisan.
stops.campa: Under the amnesty that follows the Sikorski-Mayski agreement he walks out on the thirteenth of September 1941. The state that sentenced him to death eight weeks earlier apologizes formally, puts him in a Moscow hotel, gives him clothes and a doctor, and offers him and Erlich the leadership of an international Jewish committee against Hitler, Erlich as chairman and Alter as secretary. Same apparatus, same year, same signatures at the bottom of the paper. He accepts the work.
suggested_refs: Albert Glotzer, 'The Murder of Ehrlich and Alter' (March 1943), on the release and the proposed Jewish anti-Hitler committee

stops.name: Moscow, the Polish embassy and Ambassador Kot
stops.date_confidence: Dossier tradition drawing on the memoirs of Stanislaw Kot and Wladyslaw Anders, not independently refetched. The two memoirs are cited as giving conflicting accounts of Alter's position on separate Jewish units, and that conflict is recorded here rather than resolved. Month and day are placeholders for an autumn 1941 period of work.
stops.campa: He works with the Polish ambassador Stanislaw Kot on relief for Polish citizens coming out of the camps, and on the recruitment of Polish Jews into the army General Anders is raising on Soviet soil. The question running under all of it is whether Jews will serve in a Polish army on equal terms, in separate units, or not at all. It is the doikayt argument again, moved into a barracks. Anders and Kot each write memoirs afterward. The two accounts of what Alter argued for do not agree with each other.
suggested_refs: The memoirs of Stanislaw Kot and of Wladyslaw Anders, conflicting on Alter's position regarding Jewish units
sources: Dossier tradition drawing on Kot's and Anders's memoirs, not independently refetched

segments.name: Kuibyshev, and the Grave With Nothing In It

stops.name: Kuibyshev, the evacuation east
stops.date_confidence: The evacuation of the diplomatic corps to Kuibyshev, Alter and Erlich among them, is confirmed by Glotzer's contemporaneous account. Where the two men lived there is contradicted: the dossier says a hotel room shared with the Bundist Lucjan Blit at Polish expense, while English Wikipedia's article on Erlich says they were residing at the Polish embassy when re-arrested. Blit's presence and the surveillance detail appear in nothing reached. The coordinate here is used for every Kuibyshev stop in this file; the dossier carried two values 3.3 km apart.
stops.campa: When the Germans reach the outskirts of Moscow the diplomatic corps is evacuated six hundred miles east to Kuibyshev on the Volga, and the Polish embassy takes Alter and Erlich with it. They live at Polish expense, in the embassy or in a hotel depending on which account is followed, in a provincial city suddenly crowded with ministries, foreign missions, and the whole reserve apparatus of the Soviet government. Their conversations are being reported to somebody. Both men know this and go on talking.
suggested_refs: The wartime evacuation of the diplomatic corps from Moscow to Kuibyshev, October 1941

stops.name: Kuibyshev, the letter of the thirty-first of October
stops.date_confidence: Dossier-cited diplomatic correspondence, not independently refetched: a joint letter from Alter and Erlich to the Polish embassy endorsing a unified, non-segregated Polish army open to Jewish enlistment and demanding the suppression of antisemitism in the ranks. The date is the dossier's.
stops.campa: Alter and Erlich sign a letter to the Polish embassy: one army, without distinction of nationality or religion, antisemitism in the ranks put down by command, and Polish Jews called on to enlist in it. It is the Bundist position stated in wartime terms. Hereness under arms, the same argument they had been making about schools and municipal budgets for twenty years, now made about a rifle and a uniform. Five weeks after they sign it, both men are in NKVD hands and neither will come out.
suggested_refs: The Alter-Erlich letter to the Polish embassy, 31 October 1941
sources: Dossier-cited diplomatic correspondence, not independently refetched

stops.name: Kuibyshev, the summons
stops.date_confidence: Corrected against the dossier. Four independent pages, English and Polish Wikipedia on Erlich and Polish and Russian Wikipedia on Alter, give the re-arrest as 4 December 1941; the dossier's Bundist sources give 3 December. Glotzer, the contemporaneous source the dossier cited for this stop, gives neither a date nor the twenty-hour wait, saying only that in December 1941 the two were called to the Commissariat of the Interior and never came back. The twenty-hour detail is demoted to tradition.
stops.campa: They are summoned by an NKVD contact and do not come back. Four separate records give the fourth of December 1941; the Bundist accounts give the third; a memoirist adds that the two were made to wait some twenty hours before being told Moscow had ordered the arrest. They are separated at the door. Neither is free again. The Soviet state will spend the next fourteen months telling several different stories about what happened after that door closed, and not one of them is true.
suggested_refs: Albert Glotzer, March 1943: 'They never came back!'

stops.name: Kuibyshev, the cell where Erlich died
stops.date_confidence: Dossier-cited post-Soviet archival research (Rudnicki and Mochalova), not independently refetched: Henryk Erlich's death in NKVD custody on the night of 14-15 May 1942, recorded in the opened files as suicide by hanging. Nothing reached establishes whether Alter was told. Glotzer, writing in 1943, could say only that the deaths fell somewhere between September 1941 and early 1943.
stops.campa: In solitary confinement, under renewed interrogation, Henryk Erlich hangs himself in his cell on the night of the fourteenth to the fifteenth of May 1942. The finding comes out of Soviet security files opened half a century later. Alter is held in the same city and is not told, or is told; there is no record either way. He stays alive in that building another nine months. Glotzer, writing in 1943, could place the two deaths no more closely than somewhere after September 1941. The two names had been printed together since 1919.
suggested_refs: Post-Soviet archival research by Rudnicki and Mochalova on the Erlich and Alter files
sources: Dossier-cited post-Soviet archival record, not independently refetched

stops.name: Kuibyshev, shot without trial
stops.date_confidence: The date is attested by Polish Wikipedia, which says he was shot in the Kuibyshev prison without trial on 17 February 1943, and by Russian Wikipedia. It is NOT attested by the Congress for Jewish Culture lexicon, which the dossier cited for it: refetched, that lexicon says the opposite, that both men were arrested in Kuibyshev and shot in December 1941, initially reported as December 1942. The lexicon is therefore a witness for the Soviet cover story rather than against it. The Litvinov communication of 23 February 1943 is attested by English Wikipedia and by Glotzer.
stops.campa: On the seventeenth of February 1943 Wiktor Alter is shot in the Kuibyshev prison, without a trial, by Soviet state security. He is fifty-two. The killing is concealed and then dressed up: six days later the Soviet ambassador Maksim Litvinov informs the president of the American Federation of Labor that both men were tried and executed together, an account contradicted by the archives and by its own successive versions, which move the date between December 1941 and December 1942. The public charge is spying for Hitler.
stops.quote_source: The Soviet government's 1943 public charge against Alter and Erlich, in the English rendering given by the English Wikipedia article 'Victor Alter'; the underlying Soviet statement could not be reached, and the phrase is therefore a tertiary transcription, not a primary text.
suggested_refs: Litvinov's communication to William Green of the AFL, 23 February 1943
Albert Glotzer, 'The Murder of Ehrlich and Alter' (March 1943), written while the Soviet account was still current

stops.name: Okopowa Street, the empty grave
stops.date_confidence: Attested. The unveiling of the symbolic grave on 17 April 1988 at the Okopowa Street Jewish Cemetery is given by English Wikipedia on both men and corroborated by Polish Wikipedia on both; English Wikipedia adds the crowd of more than three thousand and the Edelman and Solidarity involvement. Coordinates corrected to the Nominatim value for the cemetery; the dossier carried two different values, each roughly a kilometre off.
stops.campa: Forty-five years later, in a Communist Poland with two years left to it, a symbolic grave for Erlich and Alter is unveiled in the Jewish cemetery on Okopowa Street, against the wishes of the government. Marek Edelman, last surviving commander of the Warsaw ghetto uprising and a Bundist to the end of his life, drives the thing through with people from Solidarity. More than three thousand come. There is nothing under the stone. Neither man's body was ever found, and neither grave was ever dug.
stops.quote: Leaders of the Bund, Henryk Ehrlich, b. 1882, and Wiktor Alter, b. 1890. Executed in the Soviet Union
stops.quote_source: Inscription on the Erlich and Alter cenotaph, Okopowa Street Jewish Cemetery, Warsaw, unveiled 17 April 1988; transcribed here from the raw wikitext of the English Wikipedia article 'Henryk Ehrlich', which spells the name Ehrlich and which cites Victor Erlich, 'Child of a Turbulent Century' (Northwestern University Press, 2006), pp. 93-97. No photograph or independent transcription of the stone itself was located, and the physical inscription is presumably in Polish or Yiddish, making this English an unattributed translation.
suggested_refs: The Erlich and Alter cenotaph, Okopowa Street Jewish Cemetery, Warsaw
Victor Erlich, 'Child of a Turbulent Century' (2006), pp. 93-97

stops.name: Moscow, the paperwork corrected
stops.date_confidence: A real conflict, flagged and not resolved. Polish Wikipedia gives rehabilitation by the Prosecutor's Office of the USSR on 13 November 1990, the date used here; English Wikipedia gives 8 February 1991 and attributes it to President Yeltsin, which is anachronistic, since Yeltsin was not elected President of Russia until 12 June 1991 and a February 1991 act would have been a Soviet one. The Polish version is the more internally coherent; the English date is recorded, its attribution is not repeated as attested.
stops.campa: The rehabilitation arrives twice and the two versions do not match. The Polish record gives the Prosecutor's Office of the USSR and the thirteenth of November 1990. The English gives the eighth of February 1991 and credits Yeltsin, who was not yet president of anything and could not have signed a Soviet document. Either way the repression is declared unlawful. Forty-seven years after a pistol in a prison on the Volga, a clerk in Moscow amends a file, and the amendment is the whole of the restitution.
suggested_refs: USSR Prosecutor's Office rehabilitation decision, 13 November 1990; and the 8 February 1991 date given in English-language sources
